html:
The Indo-Scythians, or Sakas, were nomads of Iranian origin from Central Asia who moved into what is now Afghanistan, Pakistan and western India from the 2nd century BCE. The map's "Saka Kingdom", shown from the turn of the eras to 300 CE, covers Sindh, Gujarat and Malwa.

The Sakas were part of the wider Scythian world of the steppe. Pushed south by other nomads, they took Gandhara and the Indus valley. Their first known king in India was Maues in the 1st century BCE. They overran the Indo-Greek kingdoms, and were in turn brought under the Kushans.

Saka governors, the Western Satraps, ruled Gujarat and Malwa for about three centuries. They fought the Satavahanas of the Deccan for these rich lands and their ports. The satrap Rudradaman I left a long inscription at Junagadh around 150 CE, one of the earliest long texts in Sanskrit. The Saka era, which counts from 78 CE, is still used in India's national calendar. Saka rule ended when the Gupta king Chandragupta II defeated the last Western Satrap around 395.
